chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad narrated from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Ja' Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Rasool-Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The one who restrains his self from the vanities of people, Allah will discharge his self on the Day of Judgment; and the one who restrains his anger from people, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, will restrain the punishment from him on the Day of Judgment.'

key_terms.أَعْرَاضِ: Faults, vanities, or private matters of people

ai.seo_question: What are the spiritual rewards for controlling anger and restraining oneself from others' faults according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith, recorded in al-Kafi’s chapter on anger, highlights the reciprocal nature of divine mercy by linking the suppression of personal faults (a'rad) and anger to the alleviation of the Day of Judgment's severity. In Shia scholarship, 'aql al-nafs' (restraining the self) is viewed as a prerequisite for spiritual maturity, where controlling one's temper serves as a shield against divine retribution, reflecting the Prophetic tradition of patience (sabr) as a core virtue.
